title: Head-of-line queueing probe: ingress/egress telemetry and microbench notes
content:
Summary:

This doc records a set of scoped experiments and flame-profiling notes focused on head-of-line (HOL) queueing effects observed at the ingress/egress proxy boundary for streaming LLM responses. The probe was intended to identify whether small-chunked server writes, proxy buffering behavior, or kernel scheduling interactions are dominating p50/p95/p99 latency under mixed short+long request workloads.

Goals:
- Reproduce observable HOL stalls at the proxy when many concurrent streams interleave small frame writes.
- Attribute latency budget either to userland syscalls, proxy-internal buffering/serialization, or kernel-level network bursts.
- Produce actionable mitigations (tuning knobs and code changes) and a minimal test harness to re-run the microbench.

Testbed and configuration:
- 3-node cluster (client harness, proxy, backend serving runtime) on same rack to minimize cross-rack noise.
- Proxy: our internal HTTP/2 muxer (http2-proxy v2.8.1) fronting gRPC endpoints. Proxy runs with default per-connection write loop and a small local egress buffer (SO_SNDBUF default).
- Backend: runtime binary (serving-runtime v1.14) configured to stream tokenized responses with controlled chunk sizes.
- Client: synthetic harness (locust variant) using ghz for unary/stream tests and a custom binary for sustained streaming; can vary request mix ratio and per-request chunk size distribution.
- Tools: perf, eBPF tracepoints (bcc + bpftrace), tcpdump, ss/netstat, /proc/net/tcp stats, iostat, sar, and a small tcp-level pktgen for burst injection.

Experiment matrix (high-level):
- Chunk sizes tested: 256B, 1KB, 4KB, 16KB, coalesced batched frames (server-side aggregated to 32KB).
- Concurrency: 50, 200, 1000 simultaneous streams.
- Mixes: 100% long streams, 100% short streams (30 token responses), and 80/20 long/short mixed.
- Proxy modes: passthrough (minimal buffering), buffered (current default), write-coalesce patch (local dev change), HTTP/2 flow-control aggressive window update (frequent window_update), and disabled Nagle (TCP_NODELAY toggled).

What we measured:
- Application-level: end-to-end response time p50/p95/p99, per-token latency for streaming responses.
- System-level: write syscall rate (writes/sec), bytes per write, SO_SNDBUF fill ratio, number of TCP retransmits, kernel softirq rates, and context-switch rates.
- Proxy internal: event-loop latency, per-connection buffer queue length, time spent holding the write mutex, and queue dequeue-to-write delays (tracked via lightweight sampling logs).

Key findings (short):
1) Small chunk sizes (<=1KB) drove a high syscall rate and many small packets; when concurrency increased, the proxy became CPU-bound on write syscalls and serialized writes per-connection, producing visible HOL stalls on other streams sharing the same proxy worker thread. p99 increased 2.5x compared to 4KB chunking.
2) The proxy's internal single-writer-per-worker design caused bursts to queue: when one connection produced a sustained stream of tiny writes, other streams on the same worker experienced queueing delays (HOL). This was amplified by the proxy's per-connection backpressure logic which blocked at the write syscall and held the worker thread while socket buffers were full.
3) Kernel-level coalescing (TCP stack) helped only when packets were scheduled close together; in our low-latency rack setup the inter-arrival variance was too high. Turning off Nagle (TCP_NODELAY) reduced p50 slightly for tiny writes but increased packet rate and overall CPU, worsening p99 in high concurrency.
4) HTTP/2 window behavior: infrequent window_update messages from client/peer caused bursty writes and temporary blocking; enabling more frequent window_updates reduced serialization but increased control-plane traffic. For gRPC the default flow-control cadence was suboptimal for many small server-initiated frames.
5) The write syscall hotspot (verified in perf and flame graphs) accounted for ~35-60% CPU on proxy under mixed small-write workloads. eBPF traces showed a long tail in sys_write call return latency tied to SO_SNDBUF saturation.

Deep-dive notes:
- Syscall pattern: backend wrote ~3000 writes/s per long stream when using 256B frames. Proxy worker made blocking send() into kernel; when send buffer was full, the send() blocked for ~1-5ms on average before returning EAGAIN or completing once kernel freed space. That blocking time was added to the worker-loop latency and serialized subsequent connection handling.
- eBPF stack traces: the dominant stack was event_loop -> write_dispatch -> send -> tcp_sendmsg -> net_tx path. Softirq CPU was high during bursts, indicating kernel busy with packetization and NIC interrupt handling.
- Packetization: observed a large number of small TCP segments (~600–1400 bytes). When we configured coalescing in the proxy (batch writes to reach 4KB before send), packet counts dropped by ~40% and overall CPU dropped ~18% at 200 concurrency.
- Proxy buffer behavior: default proxy queue allows a single connection to accumulate up to ~128KB before backpressuring; however, while it accumulates it keeps the writer active and monopolizes the worker. We saw queue length skew where 10% of connections used 70% of outgoing buffer capacity.

Quantitative numbers (representative):
- Mixed workload (80% long, 20% short), concurrency 200:
  - Default small chunks (1KB): p50=32ms, p95=210ms, p99=480ms
  - Coalesced to 4KB at server: p50=28ms, p95=130ms, p99=190ms
  - Proxy write-coalesce patch: p50=27ms, p95=120ms, p99=160ms
  - Aggressive window_update: p50=26ms, p95=110ms, p99=150ms

Practical tradeoffs observed:
- Coalescing writes reduces CPU and p99, but increases per-token latency for the first token (adds a small aggregation delay). In our semantics this is acceptable for long-stream tokens but not for single-token short responses.
- Disabling Nagle marginally helps client-perceived latency for very small low-concurrency cases, but at high concurrency the CPU/packet overhead dominates.
- Frequent window_update reduces HOL but increases metadata traffic; tuning should be workload-aware (only enable for streaming-heavy endpoints).

Short recommendations (actionable):
1) Implement a proxy-level adaptive write coalescer: buffer small writes per-connection up to threshold T (configurable, default 4KB) or for timeout D (configurable, default 1ms). Fall back to immediate flush for short response endpoints (detected by route). Owner: Diego Morales. Priority: high.
2) Expose a per-route streaming policy in Console to allow customers to opt into low-latency tiny-chunk mode vs coalesced throughput mode. Add a flag \"streaming.coalesce_threshold\". Owner: Product + Console. Priority: medium.
3) Tune default SO_SNDBUF/SO_RCVBUF sizes on proxy nodes (auto-scale with CPU cores) and increase epoll wait granularity to avoid long-blocked send()s holding event loop threads. Owner: Infrastructure. Priority: medium.
4) Add observability metrics: per-worker write syscall rate, per-connection write queue depth, bytes-per-write histogram, and a HOL stall counter (sampled if dequeue-to-write > X ms). Owner: Observability team. Priority: high.
5) Add a regression test in bench suite that runs the mixed small/large workload at 200 and verifies p99 below X ms with coalesce disabled/enabled. Owner: Release Engineering. Priority: high.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Should coalescing be done in server runtime (closer to source) or in proxy? Our tests indicate doing it in proxy is easier to roll out, but server-side aggregation may avoid extra copy. Tradeoffs to evaluate in next sprint.
- Can we implement per-worker write scheduling fairness to avoid one connection monopolizing worker time? A micro-scheduler (round-robin across connections with a per-connection budget) may reduce HOL. Prototype idea: grant each connection N bytes per event-loop tick.
- Evaluate interaction with TLS record sizing (TLS-level fragmentation interacts with our chunking strategy). Next run should include TLS enabled tests.

Appendix: quick how-to reproduce locally
1) Boot 3 local VMs on same host net namespace: client, proxy, backend.
2) Run backend with streaming-chunk-size flag: --stream-chunk-size=1024
3) Start proxy w/ default config.
4) Run the supplied harness: ./tools/stream-probe --concurrency 200 --mix 80,20 --chunk-dist \"short:256,long:1024\"
5) Collect metrics: ./tools/collect-nettrace.sh > trace.pb
6) Use ./tools/plot-hol.py trace.pb to generate the per-worker queue heatmap.

Action items (short list):
- [x] Capture perf flame for default config (Riley)
- [ ] Implement proxy write-coalesce POC (Diego) (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4256)
- [ ] Add per-worker write metrics (Avery)
- [ ] Add bench regression (Release Eng)

Notes to reviewer:
- This is intentionally a working doc with traces attached in linked_artifacts. The bench harness is noisy; please re-run overnight if you want stable numbers. The next step is a patch that implements the adaptive coalescer + a small fairness scheduler inside the proxy worker event loop.

End of notes.
